So they remain at close range? That seems foolish in the extreme; no
wonder your gun decks are having troubles. I would build a gun deck
using multiples of the following cards:

Flash, Pursuit, Side Strike, Blur, and Sideslip - mostly in that order.
Some Psyche! as well.

Two of those cards are maneuvers, and they're the ones I'll have the
most of in my deck. My Bum's Rush gives me a maneuver as well, although
it may be blocked so it's not good to count on that.

In any case, I want to have a Flash in hand for my first combat, and
I'll use it for the first maneuver to long. Now what do you do?

If you don't maneuver back, then I'm at long range, where I want to be
anyway. I can look at your disciplines and assess whether or not I'm
going to get hit by anything; if I think you're likely to have a ranged
strike, I play Dodge. So much for your ranged strike. Now I can Blur
and hit you twice, or use either of my other additional-strike cards and
then press. Sure, you can chuck around a Canine Horde, but I won't
expect to see more than one of those in any deck; if you happen to draw
it, well, lucky for you. You get to break one gun, once. Big deal. If
I happen to be blocking you, I'll just Dodge the Canine Horde, since you
have to announce your strike first.

If you DO maneuver back, obviously you want to be at short range...
you've telegraphed your intentions, and I can use the gun's maneuver
safely; odds are I won't need to Dodge anything at long range. Barring
a bad run on draw, I'll win the maneuver battle, since I can also burn
through my Pursuits -- if you maneuver back TWICE, then it's in my best
interest to remain at long by whatever means necessary. This leaves me
pretty much scot-free to Shoot You for Lots(tm). Better have superior
Fortitude on that Skin of Steel; and if you have Flesh of Marble, I'll
just Psyche! after the first round to get rid of it.

>> They can Dodge the first strike,
>
>Only if they didnt use the guns maneuver, not to mention certain other
>effects like immortal grapple, drawing out the beast, frenzy, etc.

I already mentioned DotB, and while it clearly screws gun decks (or any
equipment deck), it's a little hazardous to give a Celerity deck +1
strength. It's also rare to see these days; i'm not sure why, as it's
still a pretty damn effective card for a lot of things.

Immortal Grapple? Doesn't worry me... that's why I'm at long range, so
I don't have to put up with THE most common combat type seen these days;
Potence/IG combat. And I can assure you I have more maneuvers in my
deck than the POT deck has.

Frenzy? Uh, yeah. I'm not going to be scared of cards I've never
actually seen played. Here again, the argument against Canine Horde
applies; you've most likely only got one in your deck (and I'm going to
feel safe assuming you won't have ANY in your deck).

>Add to that things like canine horde and the like, and there are
>numerous ways to foil gun decks in mid combat.

I'm not going to be scared of Canine Horde, as I mentioned above. So
you break one gun, once. That won't be anywhere near enough to "foil" a
deck based around guns.

I'm still waiting for the "numerous" ways to foil a gun deck without
using your OWN additional strikes, *IF* it gets the guns on its vamps.
You've mentioned one: DotB. I'll mention one: Carrion Crows, 2 points
of damage that can't be dodged. Of course, it's only 2 points, and a
gun deck can probably Taste that back, but it's a start. I'll be
expecting to see EFFECTIVE ways, by the way; ways that will help your
deck win. Putting one Canine Horde in a deck can help your deck win,
since you can always chuck it out for a free 1R damage, OR you can break
something like a Leather Jacket or a Laptop. Putting one Frenzy in your
deck is most likely a wasted card slot and a card you'll have to
discard.

>>means they're going to beat the living shit out of most combat decks,
>
>Not true. They have the potential to be powerful, but a good combat
>deck will be just as powerful ime.

The most common and most successful combat deck around right now,
Potence/IG, will get its ass *smoked* by a CEL deck that actually has
the guns on the vamps.

The reason we don't see lots of CEL gun decks is because of the trouble
getting the guns on the vampires, and how screwed your deck is if you
DON'T have guns on them. You can't get the guns on the vampires because
if you're going pure CEL, you only have +1 stealth on the actions, and
people will block. If you're going OBF/CEL, you can Disguised Weapon it
out, but this means using a lot bigger vampires, and now you have to
have both DW/gun in hand. You can add stealth cards, but taking that
equip action with a big vampire will seem real slow when Didi Meyers is
bleeding the piss out of you and you need to Rush backwards.

Theoretically, the Toreador should be excellent at intercept, gun,
celerity, with some Presence bleed thrown in. Why don't we ever see
those decks? They can't get the guns out; people recognize the weak
point (the equip action) and exploit it, knowing that one action
intercepted *now* saves them piles of hurt later.

No, it doesn't - at all. Where it does, it's a mistake.

If you do this, all it does is gift the game to the people who spend 500
quid on assembling 90 rare cards.

>If you
>have a problem with the blood 'cost' of the card, I think you need to
>tackle that from that angle

I have no problems with proper costings of cards; commonality does not
affect the power/cost ratio of a card. Many other things do. For
instance:

- clan requirements
- discipline requirements
- circumstance requirements (e.g. play when something odd happens)
- pool cost
- blood cost
- card type (because of the slots available for any given card e.g. one
master card per turn, usually)
- limiting disadvantages e.g. burn clauses (Toreador Grand Ball), cancel
clauses (Chas Giovanni Tello), theft clauses (High Museum of
Art)
- once per game clauses (Ancient Influence, Giant's Blood)
- uniqueness (The Barrens)/one per Methuselah (Communal Haven)
- requirements for other cards to be around (Disguised Weapon)
- limited in manners 'controlled' by your opponents e.g. disciplines
(Speed of Thought, Kiss of Ra), sects (Imperial Decree), clans
(Judgement: Death to the Brujah!, Letter from Vienna)
- ability becomes applicable to all (The Path of Paradox, Tremere
Convocation, Festive dello Estinto)

These can all contribute in some manner towards a power/cost ratio. The
power comes from the card's ability, the cost from all the inherent
restrictions which all cards have[0]. Commonality doesn't affect cost,
so it can't affect power - within the tolerance levels of a variable set
of power levels. That is, we'd love it if *every* card had exactly the
same power:cost ratio, but that's just not possible in Real Life (tm).

Look at Immortal Grapple. A good card, sure. But it's got a number of
problems. First of all, it requires Potence. Second of all, you have
to be in combat (which can be dangerous). Then you need to have managed
close range (either through luck or support cards). Then it also
restricts you, so if you find out that Mr. Opponent is playing Claws
from the Dead which you weren't expect, you can't play Dodge. And so
on.

Then there's Leather Jacket. Also a good card, certainly quite popular
among many players. It's disciplineless. It requires an action to be
taken, but you end up untapped for blocking duty - "negating", or at
least compensating, for part of the cost. Then it has a powerful effect
- preventing all damage from a specific strike - but is tempered by the
fact that it's continually in view, unlike a copy of Skin of Steel which
you might or might not have. It doesn't cost a blood unlike a copy of
Skin of Steel, however. Another good card, this time common.

Once a card is in a deck, all that can affect it are these sorts of
considerations (though doubtless, the list of such is far longer than I
can ever write). Jyhad was *designed* to be playable with 90 copies of
any given card - hence all the in built limitations to the game. Jyhad
was designed in the full knowledge of Magic - rarity *can't* work as a
limiting factor for power because people will just buy hundreds of
cards. Then you just create a game where newbies don't want to start at
the bottom because they know they've got to spend 500 dollars before
they can even compete - Jyhad has always been remarkably good at the
newbie curve.

Some of the rare cards are more specialised in their approach, sure -
but that in itself is a limiting factor. If something goes wrong, you
don't have a generically useful card any longer.

[0] Tangentially, this is why WWeF was so hated by some people in its
original incarnation. A generally good article, covering some similar
points to this post, is available at:
<http://www.io.com/~mlangsdo/RPGs/Jyhad/Strategy/DeckBuilding.html>
and has a good set of reasoning for a number of points.

Power is a function of cost - reduce the cost of a card and its overall
powerlevel increases.

I disagree with this, not on its face as you are discussing, but
in the sense that some cards' game effects are limited because
their availability is limited, while others' effects are pervasive
because they are easily available. I believe that these properties
associated with rarity affect the power of cards by how they
force the game to be played.

Consider:

If Deflection were a rare, only available in Sabbat, the power would
be dramatically changed. The change in power would massively alter
the nature of bleed strategies and defense in the game.
Because almost any player can easily obtain his fill of
Deflection (at least for one deck at a time), bleed strategies
are more easily countered.

The inverse is true for Disarm. Make it a common, or even a rare in
the more readily available Jyhad/Vampire main set, and a combat
strategy becomes far more effective (if only by giving Potence
access to what is functionally free aggrivated damage), and combat
defenses become more important. Thus Disarm would be made more
powerful.

How about Freak Drive? If it were common, repeat actions could
become almost as widespread as Majesty.

Speaking of Majesty, if it were really hard to come by, would
Immortal Grapple be as important as it is in Potence combat?

My point is that the availability of certain powerful cards inhibits or
expands their effects on the game and metagame, making those
cards more or less powerful. The calculus might be something like:

Total Game Power = X * X * Y * Z

where
X = Objective Game Effect (as LSJ is talking about),
on a continuous bell-shaped scale from 0 to 2, where
1=mildly useful and 2=really really powerful
Y = Rarity (Y=1 for Uncommon, Y=2 for Common, Y=0.5 for Rare)
Z = Set availability (Z=2 for base set, Z=1 for recent expansion,
Z=0.5 for out of print expansion, Z=0.25 for Sabbat Only)

So, for this model, cards like Majesty, Deflection,
and Blood Doll sit on top of the hill of powerful cards,
requiring consideration by anyone considering a
strategy that could be affected by them.
Meanwhile, equally powerful, but less available cards
like Freak and Disarm lie somewhat farther down the hill.

Of course, if you are Mr. Suitcase, you can turn this
model on its head to some extent. If you can afford to
acquire and build a deck with the less available powerful
cards, you are liable to face a field that is relatively
unprepared for, say, the 12 Disarms that you have put in
your Potence/Fortitude Rush-Freak-Rush deck.
Mr. Suitcase gets to use the inverse of the values
of Y and Z in the model above for his own personal
game power curve (thus increasing the number of
Total Game Power of cards that his opponents must
consider, while keeping the Total Game Power of cards
that he must reasonably expect to face relatively
lower).
This is probably part of the reason everyone hates
Mr. Suitcase.

- Jason Bell

For two currently played games, I qualify as a Mr. Suitcase. For one of those
games, for which I also happen to be a playtester, I've learned to ignore
comments about the balance of the game from players who clearly don't have all
the cards. While ideally a CCG should be balanced at every level of play, if
it's a choice between balancing the tournament level versus the constructed
level, the tournament level wins out. For that game, not having all of the
cards is not playing top level. (To give an idea of how rare intensive the
game is, I built an all rare deck for amusement. It wasn't hard. Wouldn't
beat a tournament deck but was about constructed level.)

But, there are several features specific to V:TES which alter the math. First,
and easily most important, it's multiplayer. Multiplayer games are inherently
better balanced than two player games due to the ability to gang up. Second,
whereas I can acquire enough cards for some games to have 3-4 copies of every
card, I can't acquire 90 copies of every card. While there are players with
enormous collections in this game, I doubt anyone has *all* the cards.

I'm not sure if there was a complaint in your post, a suggestion, or simply an
observation. But, it seems to me that it's especially important with this
game, due to the NCL, not to make rares more powerful to avoid strategies based
around rares becoming overly powerful. Fortunately, IMO, this game hasn't seen
that occur on a significant level.

Norm has explained it well, but I can do the same more quickly:

Mind Rape, cost 2 blood:

- requires you to play extremely large vampires in order to guarantee
that your prey will have younger vampires than you
- requires you to deal with all the weaknesses of playing a big-vampire
deck (Arika comes out, ready to Mind Rape, and gets Pentex Subverted)
- requires that you carry stealth to guarantee the action being
successful, as it will never go unblocked if possible
- requires that you have something useful to do if successful; you
cannot rely on the disciplines of the stolen vamp, as you cannot control
your prey's deck

With these four HUGE restrictions, it then provides a large effect for
double the cost of Govern the Unaligned.

Govern the Unaligned, cost 1 blood:

- requires you only to construct your OWN crypt so that you have a
varied age of vamps, and the older ones have DOM: note that this can be
done by using several 4-caps and many weenies
- does not require you to play a big-vampire deck with its inherent
weaknesses
- comes with an inherent +1 stealth, which is frequently sufficient
- does not depend on your predator's or prey's deck at all

Govern has, effectively, one restriction; you have to construct your own
crypt properly, and even this is easier than Mind Rape's age
restrictions. For half the cost, you get 3 pool and 3 transfers; this
is a VERY large effect that many people underestimate. Not as large as
borrowing a vampire for a turn, but certainly more than "half" as
powerful.

So, I repeat my conclusion: Mind Rape is actually *weaker* than Govern
the Unaligned. WEAKER, yes. You could look in the Tourney Archive and
see how many winning decks contain Govern, and how many contain Mind
Rape, although it's really a foregone conclusion.

information purposes:

Dark Sovereigns came in packs of 15 cards (boxes contain 36 packs):
3 slots are "uncommons".
4 slots are vampires.
8 slots are "commons".

By comparison:

Jyhad and V:tES packs contain 19 cards (boxes contain 36 packs):
1 slot is "rare"
3 slots are "uncommons"
4 slots are "vampires" (quoted because Jyhad had some library cards at
this rarity level)
11 slots are "commons"

In V:tES, the "vampire" rarity level library cards got moved to either
common or uncommon card slots (depending on the exact card in question)
but the frequency at which they appeared makes me suspect they may still
have been printed on the "vampire"-rarity level card sheet and simply
mixed in with the commons or uncommons, as appropriate.

Ancient Hearts packs contain 12 cards (boxes contain 45 packs):
2 slots are "rare" or "uncommon"
4 slots are "vampires" (quoted because certain library cards appeared at
this rarity level)
6 slots are "common"

The "rares" and "uncommons" both appeared in 2 of the slots but were differentiated
by the frequency at which they apparently were printed on the cardsheets.
"Uncommon" cards appeared at 2 1/2 times the rate (a 5:2 ratio) that "rare"
cards did. I also thought it was interesting that in all of the Ancient Hearts
packs I'd ever opened, I never recall opening one that had 2 rare cards in it.
Probably there were two separate rare & uncommon cardsheets and each was represented
in each pack of cards and one of them probably had no rares on it. Or some such
thing. Basically, it was probably by deliberate intent.

The Sabbat packs contain 28 cards and (I'm going from memory here so don't hit
me if I'm wrong) I believe there were 24 packs in a box:
2 slots are "rare"
5 slots are "uncommon"
5 slots are vampires (no quotes, all vampires)

A 4-card strategy involving Ambrosius, CW, Meat Hook, and Bum’s
Rush. It costs a vampire action and 3 pool. It requires CM and MH to
be in your hand simultaneously. It requires a Giovanni, who lack easy
access to stealth such as might be needed to ensure the action gets
through.. It does not work against Potence Vampires (one third of the
vampires in the game) – but it can also be countered by
maneuvers, by dodges (Ambrosious can’t immortal grapple) by
S:CE, by any aggravated damage.

Brujah (potence), nor against the Gangrel (wolf claws, earth meld),
nor the Toreador (majesty, dodge, maneuver, entrancement) or Ventrue
(majesty, far mastery) or Settites (majesty, lure of the serpent,
corruption, tongue of the serpent), nor Assamites (agg damage, dodge,
maneuver), nor Tremere (steal blood, far mastery, agg-damage). I
guess it might work against the Ravnos, if they rely on Fortude for
combat defense, or against the Malks if they don’t have enough
dodges and maneuevers. But the Malks, of course, can do Far Mastery

Clearly a bad option. Despite the fixing of Pulled Fangs, Muddles &
PF is far better. It only requires Muddles + PF. Your alternative
requires 3 cards, 2 of which must be in your hand simultaneously
– meaning a much higher opportunity cost and library-space cost.
Your alternative also costs 1 pool. Yeah, I know ... PF does not
burn vampires outright – but it can make it so hard to get them
out of torpor that it is barely worth the trouble. Sure, burning a
vamp is marginally better than sending him to torpor with his fangs
pulled, but its not THAT much better. Not nearly better enough to be
worth the one extra pool cost and radically increased opportunity
cost.

A deck that plans on making use of this Muddles + CW + Garrotte combo
could be radically improved by replacing every copy of CW with Lucky
Blow, and every copy of Garrotte with PF.

case PF is even more advantageous, because it can be used in
situations where the additional damage inflicted could matter.

hand. Which is better CW + Garrott, or Lucky Blow + PF?

CW + Garrott: You lose 1 pool. You can burn outright a vampire with
3 blood or less. Does not work if Immortally Grappled. Fast Hands
causes your strike to fizzle.

Lucky Blow + PF. No pool cost. You can send into torpor with Fangs
Pulled any vampire with 6 blood or less. Works even if Immortally
Grappled. Cannot be countered by Fast Hands.

>Renegade Garou/Bang Nakh.

Costs seven pool – a ridiculous investment that goes up in smoke
when it takes 3 damage. 7 pool down the drain, and you’re still
no match for Hasina Kesi Pushing the Limit with Immortal Grapple.

decks (and CW decks would be no different) is that in order to rely on
pulling the combo, you have to have multiples of each card. You
have to keep on playing the combo, or your hand jams up with CW and
Bang Nakh. Your predator jumps for joy while you bleed yourself out.

might be wiser to replace them with Dodges, Lucky Blows, or Pulled
Fangs. These are far more likely to make your Garou effective.

>your pick.

>set in mind, and the current rules set includes "no free way for
allies

I am aware of no such principle. If designers are reluctant to allow
allies action-free access to weapons, it is probably because they lack
sufficient sense of humor to appreciate Hell Hounds shooting .44
magnums. If designers are really doing this consciously, maybe they
are doing it for such thematic reasons. But if they are doing it
because they are concerned that weapons or allies would somehow become
overpowered, then they are obviously DEAD WRONG.

>access to Disguised Weapon is an OBF skill card, so it's not like
it's
>difficult to bypass a vamp needing OBF. But there's no way to give
an
>ally a Discipline master...

Okay, noted. But I’m not sure it leads us anywhere. It
certainly does nothing to show that Allies should NOT have access to
lesser versions of certain vampiric powers. In many cases they do
have such access (lucky blow, flash, dodge, arson, computer hacking,
boxed-in). Whether they can have access to lesser versions of other
powers can be evaluated on a case by case basis.

But I think the best argument that can be made against a
disciplineless version of DW is that DW is a lousy card that wise
players don’t bother trying to use, and printing a lesser, even
more marginal, version of it would be a waste of printing space. Why
print a card that nobody is going to play with?

Now I am not sure I entirely agree with the above argument, but it is
certainly far closer to the truth than the arguments I see being
actually put foreward – namely that a disciplineless CW would be
totally broken, and as Noal McDonald stated, would be “The End
of the World as We Know It [tm].” I almost fell off my seat
when I read that. I wondered, are people here playing the same game
that I am? I can only assume that such arguments are being put
forward by folks who have never tried to play a disguised weapon deck,
or who have never tried to build an effective ally-based deck, or who
never tried out disciplineless CW as a house rule. If they had done
any of the above, then surely their opinions would be closer to the
former than the latter.

I have specialized in playing obfuscate as long as I have played
V:tES. I have won tournaments using cards that most people have
little respect for like Behind You and Spying Mission. But Disguised
Weapon is one of those cards that I have had extreme trouble making
effective use of, and not for lack of effort. It looks nice, and
seems like it could be good. But I almost always end up taking it out
and replacing it with zip guns or something else. If DW allowed one
to go through one’s deck in search of a weapon it might be worth
something. But it doesn’t, and so most of the time it just jams
your hand.

The ideal use for for DW or CW is to have 1 or 2 of them in a deck
that has multiple weapons, and can thus serve as minor enhancement to
a strategy that mainly relies on getting out weapons by other means.
Anything else risks hand jam, in which an imperfect draw leaves you
stuck with cards in your hand you cannot play. But very few decks
can effectively make use of multiple weapons at this point. If you
already have a deck that uses multiple weapons AND uses obfuscate
vampires, then throwing in a couple disguised weapons might be a good
idea. But putting obfuscate on a vampire (like Black Cat) just so she
can play disguised weapon is hardly worth it. This is no power card.

-- John Whelan

that relies upon permanents. You only need 3 cards once you have the
gun to torporise most minions.

option. If you are going to utilize their other disciplines. If you
use toreadors, you can intercept and bleed, bounce bleeds, and be
effective in combat. Felicia with an obfuscate skill card can do all
of that. If you are going to put one or two DW in a deck that has
weapons and obfuscate than it is just about as good as putting in a
Tortured Confession, or any other prayer card. It might help you, it
might not.

place where 1 stealth actions routinely get through, or even 2 stealth
actions go through then it is not that necessary. It just allows you
to play with bigger vampires. With Weenies taking the action to get
the gun is no big deal. If its an 8 cap, getting the gun, and then
rushing next turn leaves you even more vunerable to speed/sneakbleed
decks.

it's a significant upgrade. At 2 pool, he's pretty balanced as things
stand - unique, good at what he does, but not perfect. Being able to
burn vampires outright when timed well is not something he can do by
design. By design, Garotte can't be put on him without some work. So
we violate two basic functions of the design and create one nasty, nasty
situation.

Violating designer intent has to be done *very* carefully. Making
Concealed Weapon disciplineless has some extremely powerful
interactions, and cannot be done carefully.

What *can* be done carefully are new niche cards - like Pier 13 to
upgrade equipment somewhat, or Charisma to upgrade allies - in a way
that is consistent with and interacts with the established power level
of the game.

three. Disciplineless Concealed Weapon removes the first two

>the alternative, which torporizes a vampire with 5 or (with somewhat
>less certainty) 6 blood (by forcing a hunt attempt).

...which isn't too difficult to find either, since most vampires tend to
spew blood off themselves like Old Faithful.

> Affected by Weapon Hosers, unlike the alternative

...which aren't worthwhile to put in your deck in quantity even WITH
disciplineless CW, because weapon hosers (except Canine Horde) will
screw up your hand very badly if you don't sit next to weapons. One
deck slot to a weapon hoser is a wasted slot that you can recover from,
but you also won't see it when you need it. Any more are actively
wasted slots that will hurt you.

>Feel free to ignore the last consideration if you consider it too
>corner case. I am merely listing all advantages/disadvantages for the
>sake of completeness. But I really don’t think that weapon
>hosers would be that irrelevant in an environment where weapons were
>more common.

(shrug) Most weapon hosers suck pretty badly anyway. Not to mention
that now you're on the X/Anti-X thread of things, which is a clear
symptom of broken.

>I don’t see how anyone can view this comparison of advantages
>vs. disadvantages, and possibly claim that CW + Garrotte is an
>unbalanced 2-card effect that is somehow going going to break the game
>and make allies overpowered. But I’m not sure, at this point,
>if that is what you are trying to say.

I believe that having simple ways to burn vampires is bad. And when you
get right down to it, it's actually fairly simple to burn vamps with
CW/Garrotte... say, by using the Lasombra? Now there's an idea.
Lisette Vizquel enters combat with you and plays Thoughts Betrayed, CW,
Garrotte. Her strike: Pushing the Limit for 4. Add Torn Signpost as
necessary, though you should catch most vampires with 4. If you can
manage a Taste of Vitae, even better.

And you don't have to burn the Garrotte immediately; you can just
torporize the weenies without the TB and wait on Rushing the big guy
until you have all the stuff in hand.

>If you are merely saying that CW would give allies different,
>playable, and appropriately powered options, then fine. I agree.

Of course not. Please don't attempt to put words in my mouth.

>That’s why I like the idea. (Actually, the main reason I like
>the idea is that I think combat should be unpredictable and
>suspenseful, and that an attacker should not necessarily know what his
>opponent is packing. I think this should be true even in combat with
>Allies. To be appropriately powered, a disciplineless DW-type card
>should be good enough to see play occasionally, but not good enough to
>see play constantly or drive out other options)

Right. I think purely reprinting CW would both see play constantly AND
drive out other options. A modified CW -- well, that depends on what
modifications were made.

>I acknowledge that they are the best combat allies in the game. This
>is only correct, thematically. Tzimisce clan membership is a resource
>license analogous to, say Obfuscate. It gives you the best combat
>allies in the same way that Obfuscate gives you the best stealth. And
>this is as it should be. But if, even after taking this into
>consideration, War Ghouls are still judged to be “too
>good” (I am not saying this is the case), then it would be
>better to fix the War Ghoul than allow every other ally to languish as
>wallpaper for want of the support cards needed to make them viable.

War Ghoul isn't broken at this point. Printing cards that break it and
then going back and making errata to un-break it strikes me as a very,
very poor design decision to a game that's already had a good share of
errata.

>But if War Ghoul decks are able to occasionally sweep tables, this is
>only as it should be. After all, the purpose of the game is to win.
>If the best combat allies cannot do it, then who can?.

The best VAMPIRES, since this is a game about vampires. Allies should
always be best-used as a sideline, and require truly heroic efforts to
be brought to the forefront.

>I’ve never made a “combat deck” that would have much
>trouble with a Garou, Bang Nakh or no. But the current metagame is
>fairly low on both combat offence and combat defense.

Not to mention that combat decks tend not to win, which is why the
current tourney metagame IS so low on such things. The extra options
are improving things though, and Final Nights still hasn't really made
its presence felt.

>At best, it is a viable combat option. By no means is it overpowered.
> For 7 pool, you deserve to get an effect that will help you win the
>game. This could pay off, but it is very risky – and the more
>people expect trouble from combat allies, the riskier it becomes. It
>does not take much to replace some of the Social Charms in your
>presence bleed deck with some Entrancements, and they can still be
>used to bleed.

Which people could *already* stand to do, and still don't.

>People are scared of Garous (and combat allies generally) because they
>it can prevent targeted Methuselahs from winning by depriving them of
>victory points. Less often do they help their owners win victory
>points.

And pushing the game more towards random combat hell is a good thing?

>> Pulled Fangs is great. A Garou striking for 8 each combat is even
>> better.
>
>For two extra pool, one extra card, and a high opportunity cost, it
>bloody well better be, in order to be considered a balanced effect.

Permanents make up for their own opportunity cost, generally. (Left for
Dead helps this out somewhat.)

>> >You have yet to come up with an impressive example.
>>
>> You have yet to come up with anything other than corner-case nitpicks
> countering my examples. In a realistic environment,
>
>By “realistic” you mean the current game environment. But
>an environment where weapons were more common, and weapon hosers more
>worthy of inclusion, is not inconceivable nor necessarily a bad thing.

The existing weapon hosers aren't, by and large, worthy of inclusion
under ANY circumstances.

> I fail
>> to see how making any of them able to burn vampires gratuitously, or
>> adding +4 damage per round for 2 pool is not "impressive".
>
>You have yet to give an “impressive” example of an
>unbalanced effect, considering costs in pool, opportunity, uniqueness,
>card slots, etc. But perhaps that was not your intent. You seem to
>be merely arguing that the effect is playable and competitive.

Again, please do not waste both of our time putting words in my mouth
like this. I am arguing that the difference between a burned vampire
and a torporized vampire is much larger than you represent it, along
with a number of other issues.

>> I do not want to see this game turn into Rockem-Sockem-Robots, where you
>> pack maneuvers *plus* S:CE and probably still die.
>
>Against one of my combat decks, this is often what happens.

Congrats! Why didn't we see them at GenCon?

>> Judging from the appearance of (so far) two brand-new disciplines on the
>> Bloodlines, it seems obvious that you and the designers are going to be
> disagreeing a lot.
>
>I am aware of no such disagreement. I am very impressed so far with

Then you've totally forgotten your multiple rants about how new
disciplines were bad for the game and shouldn't be included in
Bloodlines under ANY circumstances, so long ago. Your recent rants have
included the "if done in the standard fashion" disclaimer; a clear CYA
attempt.

>what I see on the Bloodlines previews, as well as with the ingeniously
>creative card mechanics. I’m not sure what you are getting at
>here. I suspect you have misunderstood my opinions on the
>fragmentation subject.

I suspect I haven't at ALL misunderstood what you've said in the past.

>If you recall, I was never opposed to the introduction of the new
>disciplines as a THEME, and said so specifically. I was only opposed

This is pure semantics. You were violently against new disciplines; you
wanted special text printed on the vampires and cards, and the new cards
to be printed as simply "paths" of the old disciplines. This is not a
'THEME' of new disciplines at all.

>to their introduction in accordance with the standard approach and
>standard card mechanic – the approach taken in every expansion

This is the recent disclaimer added.

>so far. I was not opposed to finding creative alternatives, and said
>so specifically. It was always my position that creative means might
>be found to incorporate the THEME of alternate disciplines using
>different card mechanics.

All of this is still pure semantics.

>It ought to be obvious, however, that the standard approach has been
>dispensed with in bloodlines. The specific solutions seem quite
>clever, and far better than any solution I had anticipated. To the
>extent that I have been “proven wrong”, I am quite happy
>about it. It is clear to me that the game is in the right hands.

Which certainly seems to be a big change from the "DEAD WRONG" I saw
recently, isn't it? (and those two words being the reason i said
anything in the first place)

It's great that you're willing to change your mind and all, but most of
us still remember you CLEARLY as the "no-new-disciplines-ever
under-any-circumstances" proponent. Trying to obfuscate the past with
disclaimers and fudge phrases is probably not such a good idea.

> and I reiterate that a
>> game which is based solely around combat and avoiding it is DEAD WRONG.
>
>Of course. There should be a balance between the various strategies
>of bleed, vote, and combat. Combat is still the weaker strategy in
>the opinion of most. Weapons are still considered weak compared to
>many other combat options.

Correct. Disciplineless CW without changing the text would skew the
game sharply towards combat being SUPERIOR to all other options, as it
would now be easy to include effective combat with a minimum of cards.

Decks would now be forced to include 20-30 combat cards, or die. This
isn't a good way to go, IMO; we've already seen it happen locally when I
and a few others were on their "thug deck" kick. It makes non-combative
decks non-viable in the extreme, and I don't think that's appropriate.

>Because, in order to be worth 3 pool and two actions, it should be
>scary in order to be worth playing. If a War Ghoul were not scary, it
>would hardly be worth the trouble to bring into play. In fact, it is
>quite possible for something to be “scary” in terms of
>threatening another’s minions and chances of victory, and still
>be worse than other options in terms actually gaining victory points
>for the person playing it.

Right. But in general, successfully getting a War Ghoul is almost
ALWAYS a good option; it generally allows you to terminate minions with
extreme prejudice for the rest of the game. You simply don't pick on
the minions that can kill it.

Taking an already-good option and making it already-better... hmm..
maybe not such a good plan.

>I have a DW / .44 Magnum deck obfuscate/celerity deck that is
>considered extremely scary by its victims. But it rarely wins victory
>points because of its pool cost. Perhaps after some tweaking ...

Right. And you're encouraging more people to make decks that splatter
stuff all over creation, but don't ever quite go anywhere... doing
nothing but skewing the game without purpose?

>I would say that DW is a reasonable card. I would say that it is the
>best offensive combat card of the Obfuscate discipline – which
>is not SUPPOSED to be a strong combat discipline -- and, as such, is
>fairly appropriate in power level. I’m not sure I am saying
>anything much different than you are.

(shrug) It's not an I-win-the-game card, no.

>> I have done all three of the above, actually. Disciplineless CW is
>> painfully good in weenie CEL decks, *AS WELL* as in ally decks. Almost
> too good, really.
>
>I’m not sure what you mean by “almost” too good.
>If you are not really claiming it is “too good”, we are
>really not in disagreement.

Well, put it this way. In a weenie CEL deck, your vampires cost between
1-3 each. Add a couple news locations for access to light intercept --
you'll never have trouble leaving a vampire untapped, so you won't need
much Wake. Put in lots of Computer Hacks, and a few Bum's Rushes to
cycle when you get full of combat. Put in 5 CEL skill cards, and a lot
of CEL combat cards, and 6 each of CW/.44. Add either Blood Dolls or
Tribute to the Master, whichever you like better.

Play as the cards arrive. You should be in great shape -- shrugging off
most all early-pool damage, and your weenie bleeders will be doing a lot
of damage per turn just by virtue of being weenies; except now your prey
can't effectively just leave people up to block, because you'll be
handing out lots of damage.

I don't think a deck like this needs to exist. It's a huge skew for the
metagame towards combat, which would push things well into the "lots of
combat, all the time" department. That bodes very poorly for a lot of
things, including variety. And I *LIKE* playing combat.

>In any event, you seem to be suggesting that if the card is “too
>good” it is as much because of weenies as because of allies.
>This seems to suggest to me that if some lesser disciplineless version
>of DW is printed, there is little reason to pick on allies for
>exclusion. It is merely a matter of making the card appropriately
>powered for any minion that plays it; either that or not printing it
>at all. Do you agree?

That's a dreadfully trap-ridden question, by the way.

One must consider ALL minions that play it, but there is certainly
plenty of reason to pick on allies, as I've shown. I believe that it's
damn near impossible to make the card appropriately powered, as the need
to balance all the weapons with all the allies, all the weenies, all the
OTHER cards, etc. create a far-too-complicated situation to resolve
adequately in a single card. At least without making it like Fata
Amria.

I think the correct approach would be to print newer cards that address
individual problems with weapons, instead of such a broadly sweeping
card like CW. Experience tells us that the cards with huge, broad
effects tend to be the ones that get broken in combos (rti, golconda),
as opposed to the narrowly defined effects.

>(BTW, I have also had the joy of pulling out Disguised Assault Rifles.
> This was in a Nossie bloat deck. It was worth it for the fun factor,
>and sometimes I actually got away with it and won victory points.
>But, as you say, it is not really good strategy. The deck is usually
>stronger without it, but it once really saved my ass against a Garou)

Oops. I never did go back and tweak it, but it was still amusing.
